purpose: Adagrasib is used to treat a certain type of non-small cell lung cancer that has a specific gene mutation called KRAS G12C. It is also used for some other cancers with this same mutation. Your doctor will test your tumor to make sure this drug is the right fit for you.
how_it_works: Inside some cancer cells, there is a faulty protein called KRAS G12C that tells the cancer to keep growing out of control. Adagrasib works like a lock and key — it attaches directly to that faulty protein and blocks it from sending growth signals. This helps slow down or stop the cancer from growing and spreading.
common_side_effects: Nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea are very common, especially when you first start the medication. You may also feel tired, have stomach pain, or notice decreased appetite. Some people experience swelling, dizziness, or changes in their lab results like low potassium or elevated liver enzymes.
warnings: This medication can cause serious heart rhythm problems, so your doctor will monitor your heart with EKGs. It can also cause liver problems — watch for yellowing of your skin or eyes, dark urine, or unusual tiredness. Adagrasib can harm an unborn baby, so use reliable birth control during treatment and for a period after stopping. Tell your doctor about all other medications you take because this drug can interact with many of them.
typical_dosing: The usual dose is 400 mg (two 200 mg tablets) taken by mouth twice a day, every day. It can be taken with or without food. Try to take it at the same times each day and swallow the tablets whole — do not crush or chew them. If you miss a dose, skip it and take your next dose at the regular time.
